report.headline: Verdict: 'Dead patent with a future' (85/100, high confidence). A neurogenic drug combo that lapsed for unpaid fees, but any real product would need new clinical trials and FDA approval.
report.what_it_is: This patent covered a drug combination: coluracetam (MKC-231), a compound meant to help grow new brain cells, paired with modafinil, a wakefulness drug, for nervous system conditions. The owner, BrainCells Inc, stopped paying fees, so the patent lapsed in 2015, about 13 years early.

why_it_died.text: The record shows the patent lapsed because the first maintenance fee, due 3.5 years after grant, was never paid. No fee was paid after grant, and no reinstatement is on record. The owner gave up about 13 years of term and had claimed small-entity status, which suggests a small company with limited cash. The scoring code treats this as dying for money, not merit (15/15). But the record does not say why the fee was skipped. A failed trial or a strategy shift are also possible. That is why confidence in the reason is only medium.

case_for.point: The field still draws attention. 56 later filings cite this patent, 31 of them from unrelated owners after it lapsed, and examiners cited it against 13 later applications. This drove the full 30/30 'field still alive' score.
It appears to have died for lack of money, not because it was shown not to work. The fee was skipped early by a small-entity owner, which left a lot of term unused.

The main compound has a real clinical history. A Phase 2 trial of coluracetam in major depression with anxiety was completed, and the developer once raised $30M to pursue neurogenic CNS drugs. Some groundwork may be reusable.
The family was filed in 9 jurisdictions, and examiners treated it as relevant prior art. That suggests others took the idea seriously.

case_against.point: Formal drug development looks dormant. Alzheimer's, anxiety and depression are listed as inactive indications, so there is no current pharma pull to ride on.
Recent momentum is weak. Only 2 citing filings date from 2019 on, from two companies. That is why this scored just 8.6/20 on momentum.

Today's visible market is cheap nootropic retail. A 30 mL bottle of coluracetam sells for about $40. That is far from a pharmaceutical business and says little about demand for this specific combination.
Selling this as a drug means the FDA approval path, which is slow and expensive. The patent only discloses the invention, not how to make it at scale.

blockers.point: FDA approval is needed before any drug sale. Exclusivity rules can also matter independently of patents. This is likely the biggest cost and time hurdle.
The original owner filed a later patent on modulating neurogenesis with modafinil (EP2125017A2) that may still be in force. It is worth checking whether it overlaps with this combination.
Ten later patents by other owners were cited against this one and may still be in force. Each is worth reviewing.
Manufacturing and formulation know-how is not in the patent. Expect to rebuild process details yourself.
No reinstatement is on record. That is good news, but the snapshot is from an archived record, so confirm the current status.

assumption_to_test.assumption: That someone, such as a CNS pharma partner, licensee or specialist investor, would fund new clinical work on a coluracetam plus modafinil combination, given that solo development appears dormant.
assumption_to_test.why_riskiest: The market read says formal development is inactive and recent filings are few. The only visible commerce is low-price nootropic retail. Without a funder for trials and FDA approval, there is no pharma business here, whatever the patent status.
assumption_to_test.how_to_test: In two weeks, book 10-12 short calls with CNS business development leads, neuro-focused angel or VC investors, and a former BrainCells or coluracetam trial contact, found via LinkedIn and the NCT00621270 listing. Ask what data would make them fund or license a combo program, and how big the gap to their bar is. Add one paid hour with a regulatory consultant (about $300-400) to rough out the trial path and cost. Pass if at least 3 say a specific, affordable data package would get them to a second meeting.

attorney_questions: Does BrainCells' later patent EP2125017A2, or any US counterpart, appear to cover a coluracetam plus modafinil combination, and is it still in force?
Which of the 10 later patents cited against this one are still active, and do any appear to claim similar neurogenic combinations or uses?
Beyond patents, what regulatory exclusivities or data protections might apply to coluracetam or modafinil products, and how would they affect our timeline?
report.disclaimer: Research and triage only, not legal advice. This report is not a patentability, validity or freedom-to-operate opinion. Patent status shown here comes from public records that can lag or be wrong. An expired patent is not the same as free to use: follow-on patents, regulatory exclusivity, trade secrets and standards can still block a product. Confirm with a registered patent attorney before acting.

signals.signal: The patent drew sustained technical attention after it lapsed, but citing activity has thinned sharply in recent years.
The lapse looks financial rather than technical. The small-entity owner never paid a maintenance fee and walked away from about 13 years of term, while the underlying field stayed active.

The core compound, MKC-231/coluracetam, still has a visible footprint. It has a completed Phase 2 depression-with-anxiety trial, a reference record in a drug database, and is sold in the consumer nootropic channel. However, the listed clinical indications show as inactive.
The family had broad geographic coverage and relatively short independent claims, which suggests the original owner considered it strategically important.

read.who_is_active: Since 2019 the only filers building on this patent are Ankh Life Sciences Limited and Intra-Cellular Therapies, Inc., with one filing each; the original developer, BrainCells Inc., has an unverified current status.
read.market_read: Neurogenic combination therapy around coluracetam drew substantial clinical and patent interest a decade ago, but formal drug development appears dormant: indications are listed as inactive and recent citing filings are few. Today's visible commercial activity is mainly low-price nootropic retail, so any pharmaceutical opportunity would need fresh clinical validation rather than relying on existing market pull.

web.finding: Nootropic Source lists coluracetam (MKC-231) solution, 40 mg/mL in a 30 mL bottle, in stock at $39.95.
Patsnap Synapse lists a completed Phase 2 trial of BCI-540/coluracetam in major depression with anxiety (NCT00621270) and shows Alzheimer's, anxiety and major depression as inactive indications.
NCATS Inxight Drugs keeps a reference record for coluracetam that lists MKC-231 as a synonym.
BrainCells Inc., the developer of BCI-540, raised a $30M Series B to develop neurogenic CNS drugs; the press release is old and the company's current status is unverified.
